label: 2D Area Formulas
overview: Area measures the space enclosed inside a 2D figure. SAT questions ask you to compute or compare areas of circles, triangles, rectangles, and trapezoids, often embedding the shape inside a word problem or coordinate grid. Memorizing the four core formulas and knowing when to apply each one is the entire skill.

workedExamples.problem: A trapezoid has parallel bases of length 8 and 14, and a height of 5. What is its area?

steps.title: Identify the formula
steps.content: A trapezoid has two parallel bases b₁ and b₂ and a perpendicular height h.

workedExamples.problem: A circle has an area of 36π. What is its radius?

steps.title: Set up the equation
steps.content: Use A = πr² and set it equal to 36π.

steps.title: Solve for r
steps.content: Divide both sides by π, then take the square root.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using diameter instead of radius in the circle formula
commonMistakes.fix: A = πr². If the problem gives diameter d, divide by 2 first: r = d/2.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting the ½ in the triangle and trapezoid formulas
commonMistakes.fix: Both triangle and trapezoid formulas have a ½. Write the formula before plugging in numbers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using slant height instead of perpendicular height
commonMistakes.fix: Height in every area formula means the perpendicular distance between the base and the opposite side or vertex — not a slanted side.

quickTip: The SAT provides these formulas in the reference box at the start of each math section — but recognizing which shape to use saves precious seconds.
